sources.news_title: United and Delta Join Southwest in Banning ‘Humanoid’ Robots on Planes
sources.text: United and Delta Join Southwest in Banning ‘Humanoid’ Robots on Planes The airlines cite a concern over the size of batteries used in human- and animal-like robots, as batteries catching fire on planes continues to be a danger By Colson Thayer Colson Thayer Colson Thayer is an editorial assistant for PEOPLE covering home, travel, and real estate. He joined PEOPLE in 2024. People Editorial Guidelines Published on July 31, 2026 12:57PM EDT 1 Comment An array of humanoid robots on display at the United Nations AI for Good Global Summit on July 7 in Geneva. Credit : Fabrice COFFRINI / AFP via Getty NEED TO KNOW United and Delta now ban humanoid and animal-like robots due to safety concerns over their large batteriesThe companies follow Southwest, which implemented its policy after multiple viral incidents, including a delayed flight caused by concerns over a robot passengerExperts and robot enthusiasts debate the bans, citing safety risks versus challenges for researchers and robot owners Two more airlines have joined the list of carriers banning human- and animal-like robots from flying on their planes. In May, Southwest Airlines took a firm stance on robot passengers, officially barring customers from transporting their “human-like” and “animal-like” robots “in the cabin or as checked baggage, regardless of size.” At the time, an airline spokesperson cited “the size of lithium-ion batteries used to power [robots] and the risk they pose during flight” as the primary concern. The official policy change came after multiple instances in which robot passengers went viral. In one case, a Southwest flight was delayed for almost an hour after flight crews became concerned about a robot occupying a seat next to an aisle — which they said violated company policy for large carry-on items. After moving it to a window, flight crews then worried about the batteries inside. Lithium-ion batteries, such as those used in power banks, have been known to occasionally smoke or catch fire, creating dangerous situations in flight. Two Southwest Airlines planes on the tarmac in Baltimore. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Our new app is here! Free, fun and full of exclusives. Scan to download now! Now, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines have confirmed the companies have implemented similar policies. United’s ban went into effect on July 23. A company spokesperson tells PEOPLE the policy applies to “humanoid and animal-like robots in the cabin or as checked baggage.” They added that the devices “often” use batteries that aren’t allowed on their aircraft. “We believe this change will help further ensure the safety of our customers and crews,” the company said in its statement. United further clarified that other types of robotics, including children’s toys, may still be allowed if they meet safety requirements such as size, weight, physical capabilities and battery restrictions. Related Stories Meet NEO, the AI-Driven Robot That’s Coming to Lend a Hand Around the House — for a Steep Price Woman, 45, Underwent the First Robotic Single-Port Nipple-Sparing Mastectomy Performed in the U.S by a Robot Named Carol Meanwhile, Delta implemented its policy on June 18. The company similarly prohibits the devices from entering the aircraft cabin or being checked as luggage. A spokesperson tells PEOPLE these devices contain batteries that exceed Federal Aviation Administration and Delta watt-hour limitations. Additionally, they do not classify the technology as assistive devices and they do not meet the definition of a trained service animal. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. Most humanoid robots can pose a fire hazard if they explode or are mishandled, Ravinder Dahiya, a professor and roboticist at Northeastern University, tells CBS News. However, he notes that it does add some complications for researchers. “When it comes to safety, I’m not opposed to the bans at all. But as a researcher, you desire to carry out your research freely, without hindrance… sometimes you have to take robots along with you for demonstrations,” he says. However, Aaron Mehdizadeh, founder of The Robot Studio in North Dallas, claims the batteries aren’t an issue. “It’s not a battery policy because the battery we used is essentially a laptop battery,” Mehdizadeh told CBS News Texas in May. A laptop battery is replaced. Getty The Robot Studio went viral earlier after Mehdizadeh bought Stewie, a 3.5-foot humanoid robot, his own seat on a Southwest flight. To accommodate, Mehdizadeh says he outfitted Stewie with a smaller battery so he could pass through security. “Most people were very excited to see a robot flying and provided so much entertainment, and it was great,” Mehdizadeh said. According to the outlet, two days after Mehdizadeh and Stewie’s flight, Southwest issued a companywide safety alert announcing the new rule. sources.news_title: Airlines are banning humanoid robots from flights. Why?
sources.text:
Airlines are banning humanoid robots from flights. Why?
More airlines are banning humanoid and pet-like robots from boarding flights or traveling in passengers' checked luggage, citing potential safety concerns.
Although humanoid robots remain rare outside the laboratory and even the factory floor, numerous companies are developing the technology, with robot evangelists such as Elon Musk predicting that they will eventually become common.
Earlier this year, a passenger boarded a Southwest Airlines flight with a robot companion, later prompting the carrier to ban robots from its planes. The discount airline announced the ban in May, citing battery safety concerns, and other carriers have since imposed their own restrictions.
United, Delta bans
United Airlines told CBS News that it recently instituted its own ban on what it called "humanoid and animal-like robots" in both aircraft cabins and in customers' checked baggage, describing the policy as a "proactive" move in case such tech becomes more widely used in everyday life.
The airline didn't disclose whether any passengers had previously tried to board a flight with a humanoid robot in tow, but said the new policy, in effect since July 23, was not in response to a specific incident.
"We believe this change will help further ensure the safety of our customers and crews," an airline spokesperson said, noting that lifelike robots are often powered by the same kinds of batteries already banned on its flights.
In June, Delta Air Lines also banned "human- or animal-like robotic devices" in both aircraft cabins and checked luggage.
"We continually review emerging technologies and update our policies to maintain the highest safety standards," a Delta spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.
Specifically, the policy bans robotic devices containing lithium batteries that exceed allowed watt-hour limitations because they can pose safety and security risks, Delta noted.
JetBlue and American Airlines, which don't currently ban humanoid robots from flights, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Ravinder Dahiya, a professor and roboticist at Northeastern University's College of Engineering, told CBS News that most humanoid robots today are powered by heavy lithium-ion batteries that can pose a fire hazard if they explode or are mishandled.
"When it comes to safety, I'm not opposed to the bans at all. But as a researcher, you desire to carry out your research freely, without hindrance," he said, noting that "sometimes you have to take robots along with you for demonstrations."

sources.news_title: US airlines tighten rules, ban humanoid robots from commercial flights
sources.text:
A growing number of airlines in the US are banning humanoid robots from commercial flights, citing safety, handling, and operational concerns.
United Airlines and Delta Air Lines are the latest carriers to prohibit passengers from carrying humanoid robots in either cabin baggage or checked luggage.
The restrictions distinguish human-like robots from conventional consumer electronics and smaller robotic devices, which can still be transported under existing battery and baggage rules.
The moves follow similar action by Southwest Airlines earlier this year after a widely publicized incident involving a humanoid robot being transported on a commercial flight, highlighting emerging challenges for airlines.
Humanoid flight ban
Airlines are banning humanoid robots from commercial flights as increasingly sophisticated machines raise new questions about how they should be screened, stored, and handled during air travel. United Airlines and Delta Air Lines are the latest carriers to prohibit passengers from transporting humanoid robots, expanding restrictions to both cabin and checked baggage.
United’s policy prohibits humanoid robots from being transported on its flights as carry-on baggage, checked luggage, or cargo. The airline’s guidance specifically identifies humanoid robots as prohibited items, placing them in a separate category from conventional consumer electronics and smaller robotic devices, reports Simple Flying.
More from AI and Robotics
See All
Delta Air Lines has adopted a similar policy, although it currently describes its ban as temporary. The airline does not accept robots designed to resemble or imitate humans or animals in appearance, size, movement, or behavior as either carry-on or checked baggage. Delta’s restriction applies regardless of the robot’s size or intended purpose.
The policies do not appear to target robotics in general. Conventional devices such as robotic vacuum cleaners, toy robots, and other consumer electronics can still be transported when they meet existing baggage and lithium-battery requirements. Instead, the restrictions focus on humanoid and animal-like robots whose physical design and capabilities create transportation challenges that ordinary electronic devices do not.
Increasing safety concerns
Experts point out that the likely reason for the bans is the difficulty of applying existing aviation rules to increasingly advanced robots. Humanoid machines can have articulated arms and legs, unusual dimensions, heavy components, and large lithium-ion battery systems. Their shape and construction could make them harder to screen, secure, load, and store than conventional luggage.
Battery safety is another potential concern. Lithium-ion batteries are already subject to strict airline and aviation regulations because damaged, defective, or improperly handled batteries can create fire risks. A sophisticated humanoid robot may contain multiple batteries and complex electrical systems, making it more difficult for airline employees to determine how the machine should be transported and secured.
The robots may also raise questions during boarding and emergencies. Their weight, mobility, articulated limbs, and unconventional shapes could create complications when being placed in overhead compartments, cargo holds, or other designated storage areas. Airlines may also need clear procedures for preventing a robot from shifting during flight or interfering with evacuation and emergency-response procedures.
The issue came into sharper focus earlier this year after a humanoid robot traveled aboard a Southwest Airlines flight. The incident drew attention to the lack of clear procedures for handling human-like robots and sparked discussion about their classification, seating, battery storage, and other transportation requirements. Southwest subsequently moved to prohibit humanoid and animal-like robots from its flights, becoming an earlier example of an airline establishing dedicated restrictions for this emerging category of technology.
The decisions by Southwest, United, and Delta suggest airlines are responding primarily to uncertainty around safety, handling, and regulatory compliance rather than to a known pattern of in-flight failures involving humanoid robots. As these machines become larger, more capable, and more common, airlines may increasingly develop specific rules to remove ambiguity for passengers, airport staff, and flight crews.

sources.news_title: American Airlines To Ban Humanoid Robots On Flights
sources.text:
More news on this day
American Airlines will begin enforcing a new policy on Monday that bans humanoid robots from cabins and checked luggage across its network, a move that places one of the world’s largest carriers at the center of a rapidly emerging travel and technology debate.
Get the latest news straight to your inbox!
New Policy Targets Humanoid and Life‑Like Robots
According to publicly available policy updates and industry reporting, American Airlines is introducing explicit restrictions on humanoid robots that resemble people or animals, whether autonomous or remotely operated. The rules apply to both carry on and checked baggage on all mainline and regional flights marketed by the carrier.
The policy text, as described in coverage of recent airline safety trends, indicates that humanoid robots will no longer be accepted as standard personal items, carry on devices, or checked baggage, regardless of whether they are powered on or off. In most cases, only clearly non humanoid, non self propelled devices that meet existing lithium battery limits will remain eligible to travel.
Reports indicate that the carrier is focusing on robots whose primary power source is an internal battery system, particularly large lithium ion packs housed in torsos, limbs, or mobile bases. These energy dense components are drawing close scrutiny following a series of aviation incidents involving personal electronics and mobility devices that overheated or caught fire.
Publicly accessible material on airline rules shows that American is framing the restriction as a refinement of its hazardous materials and special items policies, rather than a broad stance on robotics as a field. The company is expected to continue permitting many other types of electronic equipment, including laptops, tablets, and smaller hobby robots that stay within established watt hour thresholds.
Safety Concerns After High Profile Battery Incidents
While American has not tied Monday’s change to a single event, the decision follows years of industry unease over lithium battery failures in confined aircraft cabins. Social media posts and online discussion forums have documented multiple flights diverted or delayed after power banks, laptops, and other powered devices emitted smoke or flames, with cabin crews relying on extinguishers and containment bags to control the situation.
In recent months, travel and aviation communities have circulated accounts of large, life sized robots brought onto aircraft with battery capacities that substantially exceed the limits typically applied to consumer electronics. Commentators have noted that some commercially available humanoid platforms contain battery packs several times more powerful than the largest approved laptop batteries, raising questions about how these machines fit under existing hazardous materials rules.
Published commentary from aviation safety analysts points to the difficulty of fighting an onboard fire involving a device that is not only energy dense but also bulky, articulated, and potentially difficult to move into a containment bag or galley area. Humanoid robots with rigid frames and multiple joints may complicate standard procedures that were developed around smaller, more predictable consumer devices.
American’s new stance aligns with a broader pattern in commercial aviation regulation, in which operators first restricted hoverboards, then certain lithium powered smart luggage, and later specific laptop models. In each case, airlines narrowed what passengers could bring on board after a combination of testing, incident reports, and risk modeling suggested that the devices posed an outsized fire hazard relative to their travel benefits.
Implications for Travelers, Researchers, and Event Organizers
The immediate impact of American’s ban is expected to fall on a relatively small group of travelers, since personal humanoid robots remain rare outside of research labs, robotics companies, and specialized demonstrations. However, conference organizers, film and television production teams, and trade show exhibitors who rely on transporting life sized robots by air will face new logistical hurdles.
Publicly available robotics and aviation commentary suggests that many current generation humanoid platforms are already challenging to ship because of their weight, complexity, and insurance requirements. With American’s passenger network now effectively off limits for these machines, more cargo flights, ground transport, and regional shipping solutions are likely to be used, potentially increasing costs and planning time for cross country and international events.
For leisure travelers, the policy clarifies a gray area that had begun to emerge in online forums, where owners of advanced consumer robots asked whether they could bring their devices on board as mobility aids, sports equipment, or oversize baggage. Under the new rules, travelers will have a much narrower range of scenarios in which humanoid forms are allowed, generally limited to medically necessary devices that fit existing assistive equipment categories and comply with battery regulations.
Travel advisors and frequent flyer communities are already highlighting the importance of checking an airline’s dangerous goods and special items policies before purchasing or transporting high capacity robotic devices. With multiple major carriers now setting distinct limits, passengers planning complex itineraries may need to verify that their equipment is accepted on every segment, including codeshare and regional flights.
American’s Move in the Context of Wider Industry Trends
According to recent technology and aviation coverage, American’s decision comes as other large carriers and airport operators experiment with robotics in less conspicuous roles. Airports in Asia and Europe have been testing humanoid style machines for ground handling, security patrols, and passenger information services, often under tightly controlled pilot programs that keep robots landside or on the ramp, rather than in passenger cabins.
Industry summaries show that American itself has pursued a different side of automation, focusing more on artificial intelligence systems for customer service, scheduling, and operational decision support, as well as partnerships around next generation inflight connectivity. The new ban on passenger carried humanoid robots does not appear to limit the company’s own use of autonomous or semi autonomous machinery in maintenance, cargo handling, or other behind the scenes tasks.
Aviation analysts quoted in open publications have noted that airlines are balancing two competing narratives about automation. On one side, there is pressure to streamline operations, reduce costs, and address labor shortages through robotics and AI. On the other, there is growing public awareness of safety, privacy, and job displacement concerns associated with machines that look and act more like humans.
American’s ban can be interpreted as one way of separating these narratives: restricting unfamiliar, high energy devices in passenger spaces while continuing to explore automation in controlled operational environments. By drawing a clear boundary at the cabin door, the carrier may be trying to reassure travelers who are anxious about traveling alongside experimental technologies, even as it adapts its own infrastructure to a more automated future.
What Passengers Should Know Before Monday
Consumer facing summaries of the new rules indicate that travelers who plan to fly with American after the policy takes effect should review any equipment that could be interpreted as humanoid or animal like, especially devices with articulated limbs, torsos, or heads powered by internal batteries. Even robots marketed as compact or portable may fall under the restriction if they are designed to move and interact in a life like manner.
Passengers with itineraries that include demonstrations, trade shows, or robotics competitions are being advised in public forums to contact cargo departments, freight forwarders, or event organizers about alternative shipping options. In addition to the ban on humanoid forms, standard limits on lithium battery watt hours in carry on and checked baggage will continue to apply to other devices.
Air travel observers expect American and other carriers to refine and expand their robot related policies as personal robotics evolves. For now, the Monday deadline marks a clear shift in how one of the world’s largest airlines wants to manage an emerging class of technology in crowded, safety sensitive environments. As humanoid robots move from laboratories and factories toward consumer markets, their place on commercial flights is becoming one of the newest and most closely watched fault lines in the global travel ecosystem.

sources.news_title: American Airlines bans humanoid robots starting Monday
sources.text:
American Airlines bans humanoid robots starting Monday
American Airlines will prohibit human- and animal-shaped robots from all flights beginning August 17. The ban targets shape, not battery risk, despite no prior incidents. Small electronics and compliant devices remain permitted, but size thresholds are undefined, leaving enforcement to agents.
By InsideFlyer
Aug 16 · 2:04 PM · 1 min
The policy applies to domestic and international mainline and regional flights, banning robots from overhead bins, seats, and checked baggage. American cites design, size, and battery concerns, though no incidents have occurred. Agents must refuse boarding or check-in for such robots, treating them as undeclared dangerous goods if discovered post-check-in. Small devices may still fly if they meet standard stowage and battery rules.
American’s rule follows similar bans by Southwest, Delta, and United, triggered by early cases like Bebop and Stewie. The airline does not define “small” or “human-like,” creating ambiguity. Federal disability law may eventually classify assistive robots as devices, not pets, but current policy excludes them regardless of function. The policy is not yet public on American’s website, risking passenger confusion.
Travelers with robot assistants may be denied boarding without warning, as the rule lacks public notice or clear thresholds. Future assistive robots could face barriers despite federal accessibility rules, forcing travelers to navigate inconsistent enforcement or leave devices behind.
- viewfromthewing.com - reported this first

sources.news_title: American Airlines Bans Humanoid Robots Starting Monday — But The Robot Army Is Coming Anyway
sources.text:
American has now banned large human- and animal-like robots from its planes starting this week, joining Southwest, Delta and United. There’s a real concern over batteries, but this shape-based ban is headed for a collision with the future of better batteries, armies of AI robots, and federal disability rules.
The new policy was issued Friday and takes effect Monday, August 17 covering American domestic and international mainline and regional flights. Robots cannot travel in an overhead bin, in a purchased seat, or as checked baggage.
American says it has had no known incident involving one of these robots. The airline adopted the policy after reviewing risks associated with their size, design, capabilities, and large lithium-ion batteries.
Agents are instructed not to check one and not to allow a passenger carrying one to board. If a robot is discovered after check-in, they’ll invoke procedures for undeclared dangerous goods.
Small robots, toys, and electronic devices may still be permitted if they meet the airline’s ordinary size, stowage, and battery requirements. But American does not define how small is small or when a machine becomes sufficiently human-like to be banned.
Here’s the airline’s internal policy details for employees:
This new approach began at Southwest in the spring after a roughly four-foot, 75-pound humanoid named “Bebop” traveled from Oakland to San Diego in a purchased seat. The crew initially objected to its position and then to its battery, which was removed. A second robot, “Stewie,” flew from Las Vegas to Dallas using a smaller, laptop-like battery.
I wrote at the time that passengers were buying seats for robots while airlines had no real rules for them. Within days, Southwest prohibited human- and animal-like robots from both the cabin and checked baggage.
Delta followed June 18 with a ‘temporary’ policy. United followed July 23 saying it would continue evaluating the issue. When I covered those two bans, American was the only one of the four largest U.S. airlines without a published prohibition.
American’s public restricted-items page does not yet mention the rule, even though it becomes effective Monday. So the policy will be a complete surprise to passengers who have ticketed travel and might be bringing a robot assistant.
It’s certainly the case that lithium-ion batteries can enter thermal runaway when damaged, defective, or overheated. That’s why spare batteries and power banks generally have to remain in the cabin, where a crew can see a failure and douse it (a fire hidden in the cargo hold is more difficult to detect and respond to).
Under FAA passenger rules, batteries up to 100 watt-hours are generally permitted in personal electronic devices. Batteries from 101 through 160 watt-hours require airline approval. Anything above 160 watt hours generally cannot travel. Many humanoid robots are nowhere close to that. And removing one of those batteries from the robot doesn’t allow passengers to carry it.
Oddly, American isn’t prohibiting a risky battery, the rule is based on shape (resembling people or animals). A humanoid shell with no battery can’t fly. A box-shaped machine with a compliant battery is fine. A small robot with a compliant battery is fine, but we don’t know what small is and that’s left to agent discretion.
American’s memo anticipates that a passenger may call a robot an emotional support or service animal. The former aren’t accepted, and the latter can only be dogs (and not robot dogs).
Airlines already carry cellos and other valuable cabin seat baggage. It seems like removing batteries would be sufficient here. And this won’t be sustainable as the machines become common.
- A future robotic guide, lifting aide, or mobility assistant could be an “assistive device” under the Air Carrier Access Act. Federal rules define those by what they do, not what they look like.
- We’re goingt to see AI robots becoming common in the next few years. Not many passengers bring them along today, but that’s surely going to change.
Here’s a hotel staffed entirely by robots that’s close to opening. Aeroflot has had robots as supplemental flight attendants. Already TSA allows robots through checkpoints subject to screening and physical size limits.
Matt Levine pointed out in the fall that “the world’s richest man demanded that people give him a trillion dollars so that he can have absolute control of the robot army.”
Elon Musk said on Tesla’s fourth quarter 2025 earnings call that they would wind down Model S and Model X production in order to use that Fremont production space as an Optimus robot factory with a long-term target of 1 million Optimus robots per year. Now, Musk says things but I don’t think most people appreciate just how weird the world is about to get, even accounting for how weird the world has been over the past decade. It won’t be that long until we begin getting into moral questions of sentience.
In-famous non-humanoid robots are the “progressives” who like to loot and tear-down .
I’d prefer a robot in the middle seat beside my aisle seat.
It would never force me to accommodate its need to visit the loo.
Understand the issues, but airlines need to get ahead of the curve here on how to allow robots to fly. They’re coming and will be valuable ADA / elderly aides in the not-to-distant future.
